segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: I'm going to ask you questions, and we're going to talk Cherokee. I'm going to ask the questions that are written down.

segments.speaker: keith-gonzales
segments.translation: OK.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: So that kids that are going to school might learn something from listening to you talk. And secondly, so we won't lose the language or end the language is what they're fighting for.

segments.speaker: keith-gonzales
segments.translation: Yeah.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: But some of them, that's why they're doing that. I'm glad that you came out. You are a fluent speaker, you are. When you were growing up, were you talking Cherokee? And your parents were talking Cherokee, too?

segments.speaker: keith-gonzales
segments.translation: Yeah.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: How many siblings do you have?

segments.speaker: keith-gonzales
segments.translation: Three boys and one girl.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: A girl, yeah. What were your late parents' names?

segments.speaker: keith-gonzales
segments.translation: Ross and Sara.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Ross and Sara. Yeah. What is your name in English and Cherokee?

segments.speaker: keith-gonzales
segments.translation: My name is Keith in English and my Cherokee name is ah tsv nv s di, yeah.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Where were you born and what year?

segments.speaker: keith-gonzales
segments.translation: I was born in Tahlequah in 1968.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: 1968, yeah. Where did you grow up?

segments.speaker: keith-gonzales
segments.translation: Greasy.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Greasy, there are a lot of people that grew up that way, it seems like. What was it like back then when you were growing up in Greasy? For instance, were there a lot of houses by your house?

segments.speaker: keith-gonzales
segments.translation: No, there was barely, I think there were six houses. Yeah.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Did you go to school?

segments.speaker: keith-gonzales
segments.translation: Uh-huh.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Who? Did you speak fluent Cherokee when you started school?

segments.speaker: keith-gonzales
segments.translation: Yeah.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Did you have a hard time talking English?

segments.speaker: keith-gonzales
segments.translation: Uh-huh, yeah.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Did you get knocked in the head sometimes?

segments.speaker: keith-gonzales
segments.translation: I don't know, I don't remember.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: You probably got knocked in the head too hard.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: They used to get on to you back then, a long time ago, when you would speak all Cherokee and didn't know how to talk English.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: Did they keep you from talking Cherokee back then?

segments.speaker: keith-gonzales
segments.translation: No.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: I don't remember either not letting us talk Cherokee, but we have talked to people that went to Greasy School saying that they were allowed to talk Cherokee. That Mrs. Knight was putting them outside.

segments.speaker: keith-gonzales
segments.translation: Really? Not me.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: They said Mrs. Knight was doing that.

segments.speaker: keith-gonzales
segments.translation: You mean Mrs. Knight?

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: She was putting them outside.

segments.speaker: keith-gonzales
segments.translation: Dang, she was a nice teacher.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: I don't remember that.

segments.speaker: keith-gonzales
segments.translation: I don't either.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Mrs. Knight? Sometimes they would talk about how grippy she was.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: Oh, she was kind of mean. Mrs. Knight.

segments.speaker: keith-gonzales
segments.translation: I thought she was nice.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: She was hateful when we were going to school. She was nice. She never did get on to me.

segments.speaker: keith-gonzales
segments.translation: Me either.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: But she was mean to the others. They talk about Mrs. Knight when we interview the others.

segments.speaker: keith-gonzales
segments.translation: That Mrs. Snodgrass was really nice.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: Mrs. Eads was mean, too.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Did you get in trouble when you were going to school?

segments.speaker: keith-gonzales
segments.translation: Sometimes.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: How many siblings did you say there were in your family?

segments.speaker: keith-gonzales
segments.translation: Three boys and one girl.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: One girl, did all of you all talk Cherokee?

segments.speaker: keith-gonzales
segments.translation: The two were talking English, but they could understand Cherokee really good.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Yeah, so they could understand the Cherokee really good?

segments.speaker: keith-gonzales
segments.translation: U ta n and U daya.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Yeah.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: They're the youngest ones right?

segments.speaker: keith-gonzales
segments.translation: Yeah, yeah.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: I wonder why it's the youngest ones?

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: You all always talked Cherokee then. His dad and my mom, that was her brother.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Oh really, you all are closely related?

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: His mom is my dad's sister.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Well, I'll be, you all are closely related. What relation is Oleta to you?

segments.speaker: keith-gonzales
segments.translation: Because of the late Larry, right?

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: His aunt is our aunt.

segments.speaker: keith-gonzales
segments.translation: Yeah.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: This one's mom was Larry's sister.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: What were your parents' names?

segments.speaker: keith-gonzales
segments.translation: Ross and Sara.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Ross and Sara, yeah. Ross and Sara, yeah. Were they raised where you grew up, too?

segments.speaker: keith-gonzales
segments.translation: Uh-huh, yeah.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: When you were a child growing up, for instance, what did you have to play with, or did you make it yourself, or just find something to play with?

segments.speaker: keith-gonzales
segments.translation: Yes, I would just find something myself to play with. In the summer time, I would play ball.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Yeah, did you climb trees when you were little?

segments.speaker: keith-gonzales
segments.translation: Me and my older brother were always climbing around.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Another thing, did you all hunt, too?

segments.speaker: keith-gonzales
segments.translation: No, just sometimes.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: I remember myself a long time ago, when me and my friends were growing up. We would get up really high and jump off, and the trees are going like that. [gesture]

segments.speaker: keith-gonzales
segments.translation: Me and Doxie found one over there where they throw the trash. We would get up high and it would bend.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: I was hoping it wouldn't break, when I think about it now. We were doing something dangerous. What if it would've broke, we would all be living cripple lives. I don't know if you all were doing what they call the grapevine, we would smoke that.

segments.speaker: keith-gonzales
segments.translation: No, not that.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: Was it strong or not?

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Yeah, it was strong ?????

segments.speaker: keith-gonzales
segments.translation: That's why you're not in your right mind.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: That's why I'm crazy.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: That's why he's forgetful.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: I guess it's really different now than when you grew up.

segments.speaker: keith-gonzales
segments.translation: Yes, we were always going to their house.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Really?

segments.speaker: keith-gonzales
segments.translation: We all grew up together.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Oh OK, was this one nice?

segments.speaker: keith-gonzales
segments.translation: Yeah.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Did he tell the truth??????

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: Also all of Gwen's kids, Gwen lived close to where we lived.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Oh yeah, well I'll be.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: All of us played together, Gwen was playing ball with you all.

segments.speaker: keith-gonzales
segments.translation: Football and baseball.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Baseball?

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: Wheeee!

segments.speaker: keith-gonzales
segments.translation: But we would use a tennis ball.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Oh yeah.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: But Gwen had to win. Didn't he?

segments.speaker: keith-gonzales
segments.translation: Yeah, yep.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: He had the kids playing ball, like him. He would get mad sometimes.

segments.speaker: keith-gonzales
segments.translation: Yep.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Did he ever get on to you?

segments.speaker: keith-gonzales
segments.translation: Sometimes.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: When you grew up, where did you go? For instance, where did you work?

segments.speaker: keith-gonzales
segments.translation: When I first started, I was catching chickens.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Were you and Five0 together?

segments.speaker: keith-gonzales
segments.translation: Yes, that was crazy, too.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: That’s what he used to say, that he was a chicken catcher, Five0 did.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: Is he sick?

segments.speaker: keith-gonzales
segments.translation: Something happened to his back, so he had to retire. He caught them for about 15 years. Larry Don Soap had about over 30 years.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: I think it was his back, too.

segments.speaker: keith-gonzales
segments.translation: Hershel is still catching them. He's been doing it for about 40 years.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: You really have to watch yourself. When you hurt your back, it will always hurt.

segments.speaker: keith-gonzales
segments.translation: That's what my dad used to say. He was like that, he could barely get up. He would walk by bent over.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: A long time ago I worked at a chicken place. I would take the coops down with the chickens in it and set them up.

segments.speaker: keith-gonzales
segments.translation: That's the kind we used to do when I was catching chickens, those boxes.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Yeah.

segments.speaker: keith-gonzales
segments.translation: Yeah.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: One time I hurt my back, ever since then sometimes I would continue to hurt it. Even if I go like that, turn wrong, or just get up. It would hit me. But now it's not that bad, I guess because I don't do that much anymore. Yeah, really.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: What all do you all do when you catch chickens?

segments.speaker: keith-gonzales
segments.translation: Like I was with those boxes, you go inside, catch them, get on the truck, put them in there, and go back down.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: Then you go back and catch more? How many do you catch?

segments.speaker: keith-gonzales
segments.translation: Eight, sometimes we would carry ten.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Boy.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: What, did you all have them like this? [gesture] Or what?

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: I guess you all are doing that when you were catching them. [putting between fingers]

segments.speaker: keith-gonzales
segments.translation: Yeah.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Man.

segments.speaker: keith-gonzales
segments.translation: Sometimes it would take three hours to fill one truck. The boss was from Westville. His name was Red Baker. We were putting them in for him.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: When you would get to that one place, finish up, and leave, did you all go somewhere else?

segments.speaker: keith-gonzales
segments.translation: When we left there, we would go to another chicken house. Sometimes when we would finish in Texarkana about noon, then we would go to Decator. We would go a whole week doing that, going back and forth.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: In the day or night?

segments.speaker: keith-gonzales
segments.translation: Day and night.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: Is that what Michael does? Michael Cooksey.

segments.speaker: keith-gonzales
segments.translation: Michael Cooksey does something different.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: He does, like, inspections.

segments.speaker: keith-gonzales
segments.translation: I helped Red Baker and I also helped Tom Barnes with the chickens that laid eggs ??? They got really big.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Gah-lee.

segments.speaker: keith-gonzales
segments.translation: You put their feet between your fingers.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Man.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: That's why your hands are swollen, that's why they get way. Some of them get big.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Man. Yeah, what about turkey? Have you ever caught them? They say that's the most painful.

segments.speaker: keith-gonzales
segments.translation: They say they make more money.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: They would whip you when you caught them moving around. Yeah. Tom Barnes has passed right?

segments.speaker: keith-gonzales
segments.translation: He was sick and a diabetic.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: He was really nice, that one.

segments.speaker: keith-gonzales
segments.translation: The last time I talked to him, I visited him at his house. That was the last I talked to him.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: He was real sick then? Yeah, and the others. What was Tom Barnes' brother’s name when he was around? He's not alive either.

segments.speaker: keith-gonzales
segments.translation: I forgot what his name is.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: But the youngest one is still alive, his name is Henry.

segments.speaker: keith-gonzales
segments.translation: I didn't know that one.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: His name is Henry Barnes.

segments.speaker: keith-gonzales
segments.translation: I didn't know that one.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: There's three of them that's not alive I don't think. Tom Barnes and that. I forgot the other one’s name, there were three boys. There were four boys, there's only one left. Henry Barnes is the only one left, I think.

segments.speaker: keith-gonzales
segments.translation: Yep, I didn't know that one.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Yeah, their mother was a fluent speaker, just like me.

segments.speaker: keith-gonzales
segments.translation: Uh-huh.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Sometimes she would get on to them in Cherokee. Their dad was white.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: How long did you catch chickens?

segments.speaker: keith-gonzales
segments.translation: About 25 years or so.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: About 25 years, yeah. When you stopped catching chickens, did you start somewhere else?

segments.speaker: keith-gonzales
segments.translation: At the time I quit, I went to Grove. I've been living there now for 15 years.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: 15 years, yeah.

segments.speaker: keith-gonzales
segments.translation: Yep.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: Were you driving trucks or not?

segments.speaker: keith-gonzales
segments.translation: I was making water tanks.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: Oh.

segments.speaker: keith-gonzales
segments.translation: I quit that, too.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Yeah.

segments.speaker: keith-gonzales
segments.translation: I got tired.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Really?

segments.speaker: keith-gonzales
segments.translation: We were going too far.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: That's true.

segments.speaker: keith-gonzales
segments.translation: We would drive all night long after we would finish. We went to Massachusetts, it took us two days coming back. Just two of us had a license.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Gah.

segments.speaker: keith-gonzales
segments.translation: Yeah, I told my wife, “I'm going to quit.” At that time, we were in New Mexico. When we finished there, I quit.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: We got one at the house which is the youngest one we raised. He worked for a while, but he was kind of like a boss.

segments.speaker: keith-gonzales
segments.translation: They make good money.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Yeah, he was also driving by himself.???

segments.speaker: keith-gonzales
segments.translation: It's tiring.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Yeah.

segments.speaker: keith-gonzales
segments.translation: Now I use a Cpap machine, sometimes I go to sleep when I was driving.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Yeah.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: That's dangerous.

segments.speaker: keith-gonzales
segments.translation: Yeah.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: What did you say you all did?

segments.speaker: keith-gonzales
segments.translation: We were making water tanks, where Ned used to live that water tank, like that but they're really big.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: It must have been hard. Wasn't it? To make those.

segments.speaker: keith-gonzales
segments.translation: When you first start, it's hard but once you get used to it, it was easy. They wanted me to be the boss, but I told them no.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Yeah, this one would be driving and I wasn't the driver. And the others would just ride and snore. I would be driving being sleepy, the others are just sleeping.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: It can happen. One time we went to Mexico with Immersion teachers. When we came back home, I drove back by myself.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: I guess the others were sleeping.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: Weee! Somebody help, but it seemed like we got back pretty quick. I was like this. [Making a face]

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: As for your parents, what were their parents' names, for instance your grandma and grandpa, what were their names?

segments.speaker: keith-gonzales
segments.translation: My grandma's name was Katie Pritchett and my dad's mom was Emma Ross and his dad was Snow Gonzales.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Gonzales, yeah, OK.

segments.speaker: keith-gonzales
segments.translation: Mom's dad was George Pritchett. I never saw him, that one.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: You didn't?

segments.speaker: keith-gonzales
segments.translation: Huh-uh.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: He wasn't very old when he died, probably around 45 years old when he died. I guess he was our grandpa. He wasn't Dad's father, he was the stepdad.

segments.speaker: keith-gonzales
segments.translation: I think it was Granny, she had a picture of a bull standing and George was behind.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: Daddy has a picture of George by himself. He was a young man when he died, I remember that, but I don't remember him. I remember him being in the casket. That’s what I remember. I was little.

segments.speaker: keith-gonzales
segments.translation: Somebody was telling me he was in jail at one time, they said. I don't know if it was Mommy, but somebody told me he had been in jail.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: Really?

segments.speaker: keith-gonzales
segments.translation: Somebody was telling me.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: I never heard of that.

segments.speaker: keith-gonzales
segments.translation: He had been in prison.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: Dad never talked about that.

segments.speaker: keith-gonzales
segments.translation: That's what I heard, but I don't know if it's true.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: He did drink, I mean drink.

segments.speaker: keith-gonzales
segments.translation: Yeah.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: That railroad, that Kansas City Railroad, what did they call it? He worked at that place. He would leave and come back on weekends. They probably made good money, didn't they?

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Yeah, they were making good money back then. It might still be the same on the railroad. The people that have retired seem like they have it good.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: That's what he did. Retired.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Yeah, really. I don't know what they did, the railroad workers. What did they do?

segments.speaker: keith-gonzales
segments.translation: I don't know, that's all I ever heard.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: I don't know.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Uh-huh.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: They probably fixed things.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Yeah, Yeah. Uh-huh.

segments.speaker: keith-gonzales
segments.translation: I wasn't born yet.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: Huh, no not when he died.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Yeah.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: I was about four years old when he died, I remember him laying there.

segments.speaker: keith-gonzales
segments.translation: Yeah.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Yeah.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: Maybe I was three years old.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Say your parents such as your granny and grandpa, did they know medicine? Root medicine? Like they used to know a long time ago.

segments.speaker: keith-gonzales
segments.translation: My dad used to know. Yep.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Yeah, did he know a lot as far as medicine?

segments.speaker: keith-gonzales
segments.translation: Uh-huh. He knew a lot of medicine also.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Really a long time ago, it was like that.

segments.speaker: keith-gonzales
segments.translation: My older brother knows medicine, too, Doxie.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: So he knows how a little, too?

segments.translation: My dad tried to teach me how, but he said I was hard-headed.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: They say they can only tell you one time. Right? Just one time. Hard-headed.

segments.speaker: keith-gonzales
segments.translation: Yeah, he taught Doxie how to chase the tornado way, he taught him that. Yeah, as for me, he told me I was hard-headed.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: That, let’s see, John Ross.

segments.speaker: keith-gonzales
segments.translation: That old man?

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: OK.

segments.speaker: keith-gonzales

segments.translation: That John Ross that works here. His dad and this one’s grandma were brother and sister. He probably learned it there because they all knew how to do that stuff. Right? John’s dad was ???? to make medicine.

segments.translation: Really? What was his name? He and his wife used to sing, Ross he was a preacher.

segments.translation: That one was crazy, too, wasn't he?

segments.translation: Yeah, when he thought to be, he was silly????? They were very good singers him and his wife.

segments.speaker: keith-gonzales
segments.translation: Yeah. Uh-huh.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier

segments.translation: What's the other one’s name? He was a preacher, too.

segments.translation: I think it was Oleta’s brother?

segments.translation: Oh.

segments.translation: Leon.

segments.translation: Yeah, Leon.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Yeah, that's true.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: They called him Turk.

segments.speaker: keith-gonzales
segments.translation: Hu uh Boy.

segments.translation: Uh-huh.

segments.translation: Uh-huh.

segments.translation: Yeah, one time that one and Oleta sang at Brushcreek. They did good singing.

segments.translation: That's true, they can sing really good.

segments.translation: I remember when they would sing at New Baptist.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: Rosin, that one was a great singer, Boy.

segments.speaker: keith-gonzales
segments.translation: Yeah, yep.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: When they first started, he was playing Country Music with his brother Dukem. He was really good, too. He could sing like Freddie Fender.

segments.speaker: keith-gonzales
segments.translation: I didn't know he was a singer.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: He would sing his songs. Dukem would.

segments.speaker: keith-gonzales
segments.translation: Really?

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: He sounded just like him.

segments.speaker: keith-gonzales

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: Oh, Beshie?

segments.speaker: keith-gonzales
segments.translation: No, another one, he wore glasses.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: Oh, on the Rosin side? Carl?

segments.speaker: keith-gonzales
segments.translation: Carl, he is really a good piano player.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Carl Rosin?

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: Yes, do you remember him?

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: It seems like I remember a little bit.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: That was Boy’s (his name) dad. Carl was Boy’s brother. Carl was.

segments.speaker: keith-gonzales
segments.translation: Their dad?

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: He was a preacher, too.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Oh yeah, uh-huh, I do remember Johnson Ross and Oleta’s brother I think, how good they would sing. Oleta and her brother.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: Leon.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Leon.

segments.speaker: keith-gonzales
segments.translation: For a long time, I didn't know that Oleta and Boy were brother and sister.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: Oh really?

segments.speaker: keith-gonzales
segments.translation: For a long time, I didn't know, I didn't find out till about seven years ago.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Man.

segments.speaker: keith-gonzales
segments.translation: Yeah.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Yeah.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: Huh.

segments.speaker: keith-gonzales
segments.translation: I did know that Mom and Moon were sisters.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: Uh-huh, sisters.

segments.speaker: keith-gonzales
segments.translation: Uh-huh.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Uh-huh.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: And also, I'm going to tell this. Leons wife was Daddy's sister.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Oh, OK, is that so, you all were close related.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: All of us, yes, I don't think you had ever seen Leon’s wife?

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: I haven't?

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: That Leon’s wife, have you ever seen her?

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: No, I don't think so.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: She was real little.

segments.speaker: keith-gonzales
segments.translation: Yeah.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: So she was short?

segments.speaker: keith-gonzales
segments.translation: Uh, yeah.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: She kind of looked like a white woman, this one’s mom was like that, too.

segments.speaker: keith-gonzales
segments.translation: Yeah.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: They had green eyes.

segments.speaker: keith-gonzales
segments.translation: Uh, the last time I went to see Moon, she was sick. I really did see Mom in her. Yeah.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Man.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: But his (Keith’s) mom was really tall.

segments.speaker: keith-gonzales
segments.translation: Yeah.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Really.

segments.speaker: keith-gonzales
segments.translation: At that time, I was standing outside. I told my wife, “I'm going to call Moon.” She told me to call her, and I never did call her. About two days later, I found out she passed away.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Oh man.

segments.speaker: keith-gonzales
segments.translation: My wife told me that I should've called her.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: That's what happens doesn't it?

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Really:

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: You would be saying I'm going to visit somebody. They pass away.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Yeah, really, that's what happened to me one time. I don't remember what happened, I thought about going to visit. But I didn't do it, the next day the person passed away. Yeah, yeah. That's what happens.

segments.speaker: keith-gonzales
segments.translation: Yep.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Uh-huh.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: Then you feel bad, don't you?

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Yeah, yeah, it makes you feel bad, yeah.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: And also, a relative of mine Kimble, Rodney Kimble. Did you know him?

segments.speaker: keith-gonzales
segments.translation: Roger.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: Rodney. just recently I was texting him. He was really sick, he had cancer. I was texting him and I was wondering why he wasn't answering back. So, I texted his sister, telling her that Roger, I mean Rodney, is not answering me. I asked her if he had got worse. She told me he died that morning, that was why.

segments.speaker: keith-gonzales
segments.translation: He wasn't answering. What happened to Roger?

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: He died.

segments.speaker: keith-gonzales
segments.translation: He went back to Oregon. Didn't he?

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: No, Arkansas.

segments.speaker: keith-gonzales
segments.translation: Arkansas.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: While he was cleaning the yard, he had a heart attack.

segments.speaker: keith-gonzales
segments.translation: I didn't know that was Rainwater’s brother.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: There a whole bunch of them, Oregon, Washington, and Seattle.

segments.speaker: keith-gonzales
segments.translation: Really?

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: Six of them, the girls come up.

segments.speaker: keith-gonzales
segments.translation: Rainwaters?

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: His sisters.

segments.speaker: keith-gonzales
segments.translation: Really.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: Once a year.

segments.speaker: keith-gonzales
segments.translation: Oleta said, “The late Betty’s kids from California came to her house.”

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: Just recently?

segments.speaker: keith-gonzales
segments.translation: When I first went to Jay, Oleta was telling me. She was telling me they came down. She asked me if I had ever met them. I told her I had never seen them.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: They're not alive now.

segments.speaker: keith-gonzales
segments.translation: Huh-uh.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: They used to come to my grandma’s. When she was alive.

segments.speaker: keith-gonzales
segments.translation: Those girls?

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: Uh-huh.

segments.speaker: keith-gonzales
segments.translation: I didn't know that.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: Uh-huh.

segments.speaker: keith-gonzales
segments.translation: That's what I was telling Oleta, that I would like to see them, I was telling her.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: They're no longer alive.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Do you remember when you were growing up, a long time ago, when somebody passed away, they would keep them at home overnight. People would go over there and some of them would stay all night and some not. Or if somebody was sick, they would all go and help out. Did you experience that or see that?

segments.speaker: keith-gonzales
segments.translation: Yeah, I had seen that.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Yeah, did you go with them, did you go?

segments.speaker: keith-gonzales
segments.translation: I did go, but sometimes I would be sleeping. When Dunowelana passed away, I laid on the couch and went to sleep.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: He was just eating.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: They were saying to Dave, we would just be eating cookies.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: [unclear]

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: When you pass away.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: What are you doing now, not working?

segments.speaker: keith-gonzales
segments.translation: I'm working at a place where they fix boats.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: Oh.

segments.speaker: keith-gonzales
segments.translation: I start at six and get off at three.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: Are you liking that?

segments.speaker: keith-gonzales
segments.translation: It's OK.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: It's closer.

segments.speaker: keith-gonzales
segments.translation: It's about a 10-minute drive. I'm always home. I'm planting a garden now. I've got tomatoes and hot peppers.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Really?

segments.speaker: keith-gonzales
segments.translation: If it's not raining, I'm going to plant tomatoes. I mean onions and cucumbers.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Really? Man.

segments.speaker: keith-gonzales
segments.translation: About three years ago, I planted cucumbers that got this long and that big. [gesture] Yeah.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: I was just telling him when I was at Dad’s, he had seeds laying around. He asked me if I would plant it.

segments.speaker: keith-gonzales
segments.translation: I talked to him, too. He said Josh was staying with him. He said he has a little dog. They pass each other in the hall going to the bathroom. “That's all we do is go to the bathroom,” he was saying.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: That dog is old, too. It's what they call a pocket beagle.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Oh, OK.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: It's that kind and that fat. It barely breathes.

segments.speaker: keith-gonzales
segments.translation: It's fat.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: It's old. It's 12 years old.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Oh yeah.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: It's getting old, it's hurt its back.

segments.speaker: keith-gonzales
segments.translation: Oh yeah.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: That is all they do, like you were saying.

segments.speaker: keith-gonzales
segments.translation: Uh.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: Going to the bathroom.

segments.speaker: keith-gonzales
segments.translation: That's what he was saying.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: And eating.

segments.speaker: keith-gonzales
segments.translation: That's what he was saying, your dad. “Sometimes we meet in the hallway when I go to the bathroom. That's all we do is go to the bathroom.”

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: Us old ones, he says.

segments.speaker: keith-gonzales
segments.translation: Rainwater is funny.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: That dog lays in the middle of the hall and Dad pushes that thing around, you know.

segments.speaker: keith-gonzales
segments.translation: That walker.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: He would tell her to move, and that dog won't even move.

segments.speaker: keith-gonzales
segments.translation: Oh really? How old is your dad?

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: 86 next month.

segments.speaker: keith-gonzales
segments.translation: It doesn't seem like it, does it?

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: He's doing really good isn't he?

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: That one is silly.

segments.speaker: keith-gonzales
segments.translation: Uh-huh. You can laugh at that one. I don't know how old Mommy was when she passed away.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: I don't either.

segments.speaker: keith-gonzales
segments.translation: Little girl knows all of that.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: Really?

segments.speaker: keith-gonzales
segments.translation: Yeah, but sometimes we get in an argument, that girl is hateful.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: She favors the other side.

segments.speaker: keith-gonzales
segments.translation: That's what I tell her. “You're full of the Pettit's,” I told her.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: She's related to Uleskni

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Oh, OK.

segments.speaker: keith-gonzales
segments.translation: Yep.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: Really close, right?

segments.speaker: keith-gonzales
segments.translation: I think they're first cousins. Yeah.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: I don't know if your parents, your granny and your uncle, I don't know they may have already passed away when you were growing up. I don't know. Had they ever talked about the Trail of Tears? The Cherokees about the way they came through?

segments.speaker: keith-gonzales
segments.translation: No, I haven't heard about that.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Oh OK, yeah. Some of them would say, my granny told us about the Trail of Tears. Also, they were told how they traveled. Some of the elders carry what they have been told. Now a days nobody carries that. We just read books.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: Some people don't want to talk about it. It was hard to go through that.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Yeah really, they went through painful times. And we have it good.

segments.speaker: keith-gonzales
segments.translation: Yeah.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: We're enjoying it.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: We're enjoying it. For instance, your parents or your siblings, have they experienced, or seen, I don't know, talked about the little people?

segments.speaker: keith-gonzales
segments.translation: I've heard about that, Doxie said he saw them one time. Did he tell you?

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: Yes, he told us.

segments.speaker: keith-gonzales
segments.translation: He said he never told anybody.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: That's what he was saying, they were in the water.

segments.speaker: keith-gonzales
segments.translation: In a canoe.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: Uh-huh.

segments.speaker: keith-gonzales
segments.translation: Yeah

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Uh-huh. Yeah.

segments.speaker: keith-gonzales
segments.translation: I've never seen one.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: I haven't either, just u di ya.

segments.speaker: keith-gonzales
segments.translation: Yeah, u di ya.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: His sister, she just that tall. Her name is u di ya.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Her name is u di ya.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: That's the only little person I've seen. She's a little woman that one is.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: How old is she now?

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: How old is she?

segments.speaker: keith-gonzales
segments.translation: I think she's 38 because u ton would be 37 I think, when he passed away.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: Is it 40? She's just that tall. [gesture] I just talked to her yesterday.

segments.speaker: keith-gonzales
segments.translation: Udiya? Yeah she might be around 40 years old.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: Her and Josh are about the same age. Josh will be 43.

segments.speaker: keith-gonzales
segments.translation: U di ya is about that age.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: She works at the nursing home. Our aunt is in there, she struggles with her.

segments.speaker: keith-gonzales
segments.translation: That's what she was saying.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: Boy, she has some big kids.

segments.speaker: keith-gonzales
segments.translation: Have seen Caleb? When I see him, he reminds me of u ton.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: They're tall and big.

segments.speaker: keith-gonzales
segments.translation: Dillion is round.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: Their dad is little, too. He's just about that tall [gesture] and they have kids that big. [gesture]

segments.speaker: keith-gonzales
segments.translation: That Ellie is full of u di ya. That time we were eating, Doxie said Ellie was saying, “Have you seen Angie?” Doxie asked her who, who is that? She said, my mom.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: Yes, that's what she calls her. Her name is Angela in English but she calls her Angie. She won't call her Mommy, it's Angie. I don't know why she does that.

segments.speaker: keith-gonzales
segments.translation: I don't know why. She goes to Westville school.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: Ellie? Why that far?

segments.speaker: keith-gonzales
segments.translation: U di ya said that's where she wanted to go to school. She wanted to go to school here.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: Sequoyah?

segments.speaker: keith-gonzales
segments.translation: But she changed her mind and went to Westville.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: They have to go a long ways.

segments.speaker: keith-gonzales
segments.translation: She rides the bus. They meet the bus in Stilwell.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: They take them from there, she sure is the boss. Right? Does your wife can when you make a garden?

segments.speaker: keith-gonzales
segments.translation: She won't even get out of the house. Now that it's going to warm up you won't see her outside.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: She gets hot?

segments.speaker: keith-gonzales
segments.translation: She can go out for five minutes and starts sweating. She's a diabetic.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: That's what you were telling me.

segments.speaker: keith-gonzales
segments.translation: She takes 11 pills a day, I have to take care of her when she gets sick.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: They might be giving her too much.

segments.speaker: keith-gonzales
segments.translation: She also gives herself shots when she gets up in the morning and before the evening. Her legs are just that big.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: You know I went eight years, I was giving myself four shots a day. For eight years, I gave myself those shots. Last year my sugar was getting low from the shots. I decided to stop so it's been a year. I don't give myself shots anymore. I just take Metformin in the morning and evening. It will make you fat. That insulin will make you fat.

segments.speaker: keith-gonzales
segments.translation: Yeah, this one is fat.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: I didn't know that. When I stopped the shots, I lost weight really quick. I asked the doctor why I lost weight so fast. He said if you're getting the shots, it will make you gain weight. The Novolog, do you give yourself shots? He said Novolog will do that to you.

segments.speaker: keith-gonzales
segments.translation: I forgot what this one uses for her shots, she's kind of fat.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: That's why. Especially I was giving myself four shots a day. Morning, noon, evening, and night. God, I was tired. I was giving them in my stomach.

segments.speaker: keith-gonzales
segments.translation: Sometimes my wife will raise her shirt, she would have a bruise where she gave herself a shot.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: Sometimes that would happen to me.

segments.speaker: keith-gonzales
segments.translation: Sometimes I have to help her hold her arm so she can give herself a shot.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: I can't do it there.

segments.speaker: keith-gonzales
segments.translation: She wanted me to give her the shot, I told her no.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: But that needle is real little.

segments.speaker: keith-gonzales
segments.translation: Yeah it's about that big.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: The amount of insulin?

segments.speaker: keith-gonzales
segments.translation: Yeah.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: That much.

segments.speaker: keith-gonzales
segments.translation: There was a good portion.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: I did five units four times a day.

segments.speaker: keith-gonzales
segments.translation: This one puts a lot in them. I hold her arm on her fat. I do her like this, [gesture] then she gives herself a shot.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: Dad does the same thing. He has it almost full.

segments.speaker: keith-gonzales
segments.translation: She wanted me to give her a shot, I told her no. I told her, “I'm not a doctor.”

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: I can't give myself a shot here. Granny, do you remember Granny u lu tse? Where was it? She would give herself a shot here. And also here and everywhere, but I didn't like to give myself a shot there. Granny was like that, wasn't she?

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: My sugar got a little high, too, the average was 200. One time, what's David's name in Cherokee?

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: U sk ni, I told him that's a good name for him.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: He gave me some medicine, but it was for something else, for my coughing. I boiled it and started drinking it. My sugar started going down. Sometimes in the morning it would just be 98, and sometimes it would get to 111. At first, it would be high but now it's low. This morning it was 118, and I ate a lot last night.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: You’re doing good.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: I'm doing pretty good. I don't know if that's helping me.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: It might. If mine was 98, I'd be passed out somewhere.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: One time it was 88, that scared me. I immediately went to look for something sweet.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: I told my doctor when my sugar gets low, I look for something sweet and enjoy it. She said I bet you are. You're really liking it.

segments.speaker: keith-gonzales
segments.translation: That's what my wife does.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: To be honest, you're supposed to use orange juice, it's really fast.

segments.speaker: keith-gonzales
segments.translation: She eats bananas, too.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: A banana will raise it real quick.

segments.speaker: keith-gonzales
segments.translation: She told me to get her some bananas the other day. But don't be climbing on the trees. She got mad at me.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: Does she not talk Cherokee?

segments.speaker: keith-gonzales
segments.translation: I talk Cherokee to her and she can understand a little bit of it. But she forgets it. I tell her she's a Mexican.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: So are you a Mexican?

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Yeah, do you read Cherokee?

segments.speaker: keith-gonzales
segments.translation: I don't know how.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: You don't? What about your parents? Did they know how to read Cherokee?

segments.speaker: keith-gonzales
segments.translation: I never noticed it, but my dad probably knew how. But I never seen it.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: You say you grew up over there, and when you moved North did they talk different? Did they talk different from there to here?

segments.speaker: keith-gonzales
segments.translation: Yes, yep.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: Different?

segments.speaker: keith-gonzales
segments.translation: You would understand more Cherokee if you go to Bell. Won't you?

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: Really.

segments.speaker: keith-gonzales
segments.translation: They talk a lot of Cherokee, the young kids will talk Cherokee to you.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: They talk the old way.

segments.speaker: keith-gonzales
segments.translation: The old way.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: You mean the people from Bell? There was a time, where the Nofires lived. There was a long hill. What was it called?

segments.speaker: keith-gonzales
segments.translation: Kirk Mountain?

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: No, there was a church. What was the name?

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: There at Bell?

segments.speaker: keith-gonzales
segments.translation: One is Kirk Mountain.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: The church, Salem?

segments.speaker: keith-gonzales
segments.translation: Salem Baptist Church?

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: It was on top of the hill, where the Nofires live. Oak Grove. No, it's not Oak Grove.

segments.speaker: keith-gonzales
segments.translation: I think that’s toward Kirk Mountain.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: I know what you're talking about, it's Oak something.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: There was kids there talking all in Cherokee. I guess all the Nofires lived there.

segments.speaker: keith-gonzales
segments.translation: You won't hear anybody talking Cherokee in Grove.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: You don't?

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Just in English.

segments.speaker: keith-gonzales
segments.translation: I was telling my wife that’s why I'm losing the Cherokee. I might lose it all.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: I’m just going to save it. If you start talking English, we're going to run you off.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: But really, the names of things are different, too, where I'm from. And this way. One time we were talking about cars, somebody said, “Oh that digtuleni” and they said, “Oh, they're talking about you.” So here they call cars digtuleni.

segments.speaker: keith-gonzales
segments.translation: I just say digtuleni.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Yeah, really.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: Some people say four wheels, don't they?

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Some of them say rubber tires. That's how different we talk.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: When they were little boys, do you remember we were at Grannys? You and Doxie went to the creek. Their mom gave me a stick to get the boys with and me acting like a grown up. I went down, they chased me back up. They chased me back up. They said, “Look at that, they chased her back and she's supposed to bring them back.”

segments.speaker: keith-gonzales
segments.translation: No I don't remember that.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: I remember when you all chased me back. I was running away with the switch. They scared me. Everybody thought it was really funny. They were saying, “She thought she was tough and got chased back.”

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Like you all are saying and talking about. Sometimes it's good to think about when we grew up a long time ago and the way it was like growing up, and nowadays it's very different than when I was growing up and where I was born. I was born in Euchi, but now it's covered with water - there's a lake there now.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: Same as where Granny used to live. Right?

segments.speaker: keith-gonzales
segments.translation: Yeah, that log house.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: There's water there.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: When you was growing up as a boy, when you think about it, was the house small where you grew up?

segments.speaker: keith-gonzales
segments.translation: A log house, yep.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: There were only two rooms, wasn't it?

segments.speaker: keith-gonzales
segments.translation: There was a living room when you went in. On this side was a big bedroom, a kitchen, and bathroom. That's all it was.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: When I think about it now, I wonder how we did it. When you see that little house. Did you have running water, what about lights like this? You had all of that when you were growing up. As you were growing up.

segments.speaker: keith-gonzales
segments.translation: In the winter, it was really warm in the house.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Yeah.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: I guess your dad built that, didn't he?

segments.speaker: keith-gonzales
segments.translation: Yeah, by himself in 1968. That's when I was born. He wrote it down in the cement.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Is the building still there right now?

segments.speaker: keith-gonzales
segments.translation: No, we tore it down.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: You tore it down?

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: They built an Indian home there, didn't they?

segments.speaker: keith-gonzales
segments.translation: Where our Indian home is now, is where our garden used to be. When we lived in that log house, they told us we had to tear it down. At that time Cherokee Nation gave me a trailer. Oh, that's where that house was. And that one was a good gardener. Wasn't he?

segments.speaker: keith-gonzales
segments.translation: Yep.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: Your dad.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Yep, so they cover your garden spot.

segments.speaker: keith-gonzales
segments.translation: Yeah, he moved to the other side.? His garden kept getting bigger.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: So, it kept making a bigger spot for you to work in.

segments.speaker: keith-gonzales
segments.translation: Yep, I was always going in there and eating tomatoes.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Gah-lee, I bet they were really good. Right? Did you take some salt with you?

segments.speaker: keith-gonzales
segments.translation: Salt, yep. Those cherry tomatoes.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Gah-lee man.

segments.speaker: keith-gonzales
segments.translation: Or cucumbers. I mean tomatoes.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: I couldn't eat cucumbers because I would get boils.

segments.speaker: keith-gonzales
segments.translation: Yep, Rod, too, he always got them on his butt. And you, too. Ain't it?

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: I would just be like this and Dad would tell me to walk right. When you grow up that's how you're going to walk. I would tell him I can't. And Granny was doctoring us. “Granny!” I would be hollering.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Me too, one time I got one coming out on my butt. I was working for the County using a back hoe, gah-lee, when I would start digging, man, it would hurt.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: They will make you sick. Rod moved up there by Dad’s.

segments.speaker: keith-gonzales
segments.translation: Really? I'd like to see him.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: He's bringing a trailer. As soon as he saw me, he said, “Sis, do you still get boils?”

segments.speaker: keith-gonzales
segments.translation: Rod? I would like to see him. The last time I seen him was when Dad passed away. He came over.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: How long was he in there? Our kin folk said he was in prison.

segments.speaker: keith-gonzales
segments.translation: I don't know if it was three years or five years. Rainwater was telling me.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: He looks really old, but it seems like he's doing good.

segments.speaker: keith-gonzales
segments.translation: He said he didn't have any teeth.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: He said he started going to church now. You know Joe Christie? His son.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Oh. What's his name?

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: His name is Rodney.

segments.speaker: keith-gonzales
segments.translation: He not married to Sandy, is he?

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: He has another woman.

segments.speaker: keith-gonzales
segments.translation: Yeah, that's what your dad said.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: He said they were going to get married.

segments.speaker: keith-gonzales
segments.translation: Really?

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: Joe is supposed to marry them.

segments.speaker: keith-gonzales
segments.translation: Joe Christie, really? I was telling Doxie that I would like to see Rod again.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: He's still the same as always, Rod was always nice. Wasn't he?

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: That Joe Christie you're talking about, is he a preacher?

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: Uh-huh. You know him, don't you?

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Yeah, I know him. What's his son’s name?

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: Rodney, Rodney Pritchett. But he has other boys.

segments.speaker: keith-gonzales
segments.translation: One was Bimbo Christie, that one was killed by a car at Cherry Tree.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: So there's still one more?

segments.speaker: keith-gonzales
segments.translation: That's the only one I knew, there's still another one. That time Cherokee Nation was putting in a water line, I saw him there.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: There's a girl, I think.

segments.speaker: keith-gonzales
segments.translation: I don't know.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: That's Joe’s child.

segments.speaker: keith-gonzales
segments.translation: That's what Mommy was saying, that one working outside is Rod’s dad, and the one with him is his son. She said, “I didn't know that.”

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Does one of them play music or sing, that Joe’s son you all are talking about?

segments.speaker: keith-gonzales
segments.translation: No telling.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: I think so, it’s not Rod. It would be a different one. I think there is one that plays music.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Also, the one we're talking about has a boy that plays music, too, I think. Maybe I'm thinking about someone else.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: You're thinking about someone else.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: That, uh, I forget the name, ha, I forget their names.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: Me too.

segments.speaker: keith-gonzales
segments.translation: We're getting old.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Yeah, especially me. I'm getting so forgetful. This is the last thing I'm going to ask you. Do you think the Cherokee language is going to fade away?

segments.speaker: keith-gonzales
segments.translation: I don't think so, the elders used to talk about that. I remember when I was in grade school, they were saying the Cherokee was going to end. But I don't think so.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Yeah, really. This school here is teaching them Cherokee. They talk a little different.

segments.speaker: keith-gonzales
segments.translation: It would be good if we don't lose it.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: They don't talk like we talk. When we were growing up, we don't talk Cherokee like they did either. It really is kind of changing.

segments.speaker: keith-gonzales
segments.translation: Ned didn't understand English. Somebody had to help him.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: My uncle.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Really, yeah.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: Do you know what his name was in English? Roach Killer.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Roach Killer,

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: Ain't it?

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: We were asking why his mom would do that. He was my grandfathers half brother, his name was Roach Killer.

segments.speaker: keith-gonzales
segments.translation: He didn't understand Cherokee.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: He didn't? He always had to have a translator?

segments.speaker: keith-gonzales
segments.translation: And Charlie Cochran from Bell, he didn't understand English either.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: I wonder why Ned was that way, duda could talk English good.

segments.speaker: keith-gonzales
segments.translation: I don't know why.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: He really didn't understand English.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Some of them would just tease each other. Some of them don't talk English is what they say. If they won't credit then they will talk.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: They would say charge it.

segments.speaker: keith-gonzales
segments.translation: John Ross’s sister May Jean Ross, when we were in high school and grade school, you would never hear her talking English. Her cousin Roxann Dick, when they would get by themselves, they would talk English to each other.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: I guess they were embarrassed.

segments.speaker: keith-gonzales
segments.translation: They were embarrassed.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: To talk English.

segments.speaker: keith-gonzales
segments.translation: They told them, “You all talk English when you're by yourselves, but when someone speaks to you in English, you won't talk.”

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: They were embarrassed. I saw them awhile back, they were here and she was talking English.

segments.speaker: keith-gonzales
segments.translation: May Jean, really? I guess she grew up. Who was she with, Bordy?

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: All of her sisters.

segments.speaker: keith-gonzales
segments.translation: Sally and Emma.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: Sally and Emma.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Yeah.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: They were all talking in English.

segments.speaker: keith-gonzales
segments.translation: Really? I'm surprised.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: I'm going to ask why they say they forgot to talk Cherokee. What do you think when they say that? Do they really forget?

segments.speaker: keith-gonzales
segments.translation: I believe it.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: It's almost happened to you?

segments.speaker: keith-gonzales
segments.translation: It almost happened to me.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: When I was growing up, Cherokee was all we talked. I barely learned English. I'm still learning.

segments.speaker: keith-gonzales
segments.translation: When me and Doxie talk we speak in Cherokee, and sometimes I would run out. I would start talking in English.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Yeah, I grew up when the elders were around. I didn't hardly learn to talk English, just enough to get through. I grew up with everybody talking Cherokee.

segments.speaker: keith-gonzales
segments.translation: John Ross’s mom Gahugi didn't understand English either. I forgot her, too, her name was Nancy Ross. I didn't know what their dad was like, John. I didn't know if he could understand English.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: I don't know. All I talked to him was in Cherokee.

segments.speaker: keith-gonzales
segments.translation: Me too, they had a homemade fly swat. Do you remember that? Those things they use for fishing poles and the tongue from the work boots. They made a fly swat with that.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: Really?

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: He cut the work boot.

segments.speaker: keith-gonzales
segments.translation: The tongue was about this big, [gesture] and he would hang it on the fly swat.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: He was using that?

segments.speaker: keith-gonzales
segments.translation: He was using that, yeah.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Boy that was smart.

segments.speaker: keith-gonzales
segments.translation: They never had a push mower, he used a weed hook outside to cut the grass.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: They also had.

segments.speaker: keith-gonzales
segments.translation: The old ones.

segments.speaker: dianna-guffey
segments.translation: Yes, the old ones.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: I have one of those, sometimes I push it around.

segments.speaker: keith-gonzales
segments.translation: Sometimes I see them at a flea market.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Well I'm glad we got to talk all in Cherokee.
